title: Stasimon 1 (lines 480–511)

teacherSummary.text: The Chorus imagines the unknown killer fleeing like a wild bull, pursued by Apollo's voice. They are troubled by Teiresias' words but will not believe them against Oedipus without proof.

vocabulary.definition: tested to measure quality, as gold is tested
vocabulary.context:
Or how without sign assured, can I blame
Him who saved our State when the wingèd songstress came,
Tested and tried in the light of us all, like gold assayed?
vocabulary.source: Liber et Libri contextual definition, hand-written against the line in Oedipus Rex

context.history: A stasimon is a choral ode sung between episodes. Delphi was believed to be the centre ("mid shrine") of the earth.

significance: The hunted bull is an image of Oedipus himself, though the Chorus does not know it. Their loyalty and demand for evidence show a fair-minded community.
discussionQuestions: How much evidence should we need before we believe an accusation against someone we trust?
Where does imagery appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with leadership and the city?

Yea, but now flashed forth the summons from Parnassus’ snowy peak,
“Near and far the undiscovered doer of this murder seek!”
Now like a sullen bull he roves
Through forest brakes and upland groves,
And vainly seeks to fly
The doom that ever nigh
Flits o’er his head,
Still by the avenging Phoebus sped,
The voice divine,
From Earth’s mid shrine.

anchorPassages.note: Loyalty and doubt: the elders refuse to convict without sign, remembering past salvation.
anchorPassages.text:
Sore perplexèd am I by the words of the master seer.
Are they true, are they false? I know not and bridle my tongue for fear,
Fluttered with vague surmise; nor present nor future is clear.
Quarrel of ancient date or in days still near know I none
Twixt the Labdacidan house and our ruler, Polybus’ son.
Proof is there none: how then can I challenge our King’s good name,
How in a blood-feud join for an untracked deed of shame?
All wise are Zeus and Apollo, and nothing is hid from their ken;
They are gods; and in wits a man may surpass his fellow men;
But that a mortal seer knows more than I know—where
Hath this been proven? Or how without sign assured, can I blame
Him who saved our State when the wingèd songstress came,
Tested and tried in the light of us all, like gold assayed?
How can I now assent when a crime is on Oedipus laid?

items.text: Which image in Stasimon 1 best captures the murderer's plight: the sullen bull or the sleuth-hounds? Defend your choice.

A strong answer may prefer the bull for its loneliness, but it should explain which image better fits the ode's claim that the doom "ever nigh / Flits o'er his head" (lines 493–494).

items.text: Compare how “Stasimon 1 (lines 480–511)” treats the hunted man with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Oedipus Rex see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A cross-text synthesis.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The Chorus is fair-minded: it believes the oracle but will not condemn the king without proof. Useful evidence: “Proof is there none: how then can I challenge our King’s good name, / How in a blood-feud join for an untracked deed of shame” (Stasimon 1, lines 503–504): The elders will not accuse the king who saved them without evidence, which shows a fair-minded loyalty. On theme: The ode weighs the authority of a prophet against loyalty to a king who saved the city, and asks what counts as proof. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.
